question: Move the AED at DREAM Charter Elementary and Middle School into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: DREAM Charter Elementary and Middle School (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "Third Floor; Main Entrance/Lobby".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.18 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 8 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 11 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists The Mount Sinai Hospital, a hospital normally staffed around the clock, 184 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving DREAM Charter's AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in emergency access. The school's current location is reachable only 55 of 168 hours during the school year [E3], and the area experienced 1.18 cardiac-arrest calls annually during hours when every nearby AED was closed [E4]. Citywide, only 1.4 percent of actual call locations had access to a confirmed open AED [E6]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED reaches 66.5 percent survival versus 43.0 percent without [E7]. This school-wall cabinet could meaningfully improve those odds for the neighborhood.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on real data showing a gap, but several uncertainties undermine confidence in this specific fix. Yes, the area saw 1.18 calls yearly during closed-AED hours [E4], but we don't know where those calls actually occurred within the ZIP code [E9]—they may not have been near DREAM Charter at all. The 11 other AEDs nearby [E5] could serve some of those events if their hours were extended instead, which might cost less. Mount Sinai Hospital sits only 184 meters away [E8] and is staffed 24/7, making it a potential alternative host worth exploring before committing to a school-wall cabinet. We also lack critical information: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school permits after-hours access, and whether the school would maintain it [E9]. The survival benefit from public AEDs is real [E7], but we cannot confirm this location would reach the actual call sites.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we don't know the exact location of those 1.18 annual calls within the ZIP [E9], and Mount Sinai's 24/7 staffing is worth exploring [E8]. However, the skeptic's suggestion to extend hours at the 11 nearby AEDs assumes those sites are willing and able to do so—we have no evidence they are. DREAM Charter's street wall, by contrast, is a concrete opportunity: it sits within the two-minute walking radius where the calls occurred, and moving it there costs only the cabinet itself, not negotiating with 11 separate organizations. The survival gap is stark—1.4 percent of actual call locations citywide had access to an open AED [E6]—and a school building's exterior is a defensible, visible location. Before pursuing Mount Sinai, the city should confirm whether DREAM Charter's proposal is feasible [E9] and whether it would genuinely serve the neighborhood's cardiac-arrest risk.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point: negotiating with 11 separate AED sites to extend their hours may be harder than installing one cabinet at DREAM Charter. But that's an assumption, not evidence. We don't know the actual cost of the cabinet, maintenance burden, or vandalism risk [E9]—factors that could make the school-wall option more expensive or unreliable than it appears. More importantly, we still cannot confirm those 1.18 annual calls [E4] occurred near DREAM Charter rather than elsewhere in the ZIP [E9]. Mount Sinai's 184-meter proximity and round-the-clock staffing [E8] offer a concrete alternative worth testing first. Before committing resources to a school cabinet, the city should map where those calls actually happened and whether Mount Sinai or extending existing AED hours would reach them more cost-effectively.

verdict.summary: Real gap exists (1.18 calls/year during closed-AED hours [E4]), but call locations within ZIP unknown [E9]. Mount Sinai alternative [E8] and cost/maintenance unknowns [E9] require investigation before committing to school-wall cabinet.
verdict.strongestFor: Area experiences 1.18 annual cardiac arrests during all-AED-closed hours [E4]; public AED shock yields 66.5% survival vs 43.0% [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual call locations within ZIP unknown [E9]; Mount Sinai Hospital 184 m away staffed 24/7 [E8]; cabinet cost, vandalism, maintenance, school access all unknown [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Map 2025 cardiac-arrest call locations within ZIP; confirm Mount Sinai AED availability; obtain cabinet cost and school access feasibility.
